content.title: Thanks, and paper withdrawal
content.comment:
Dear organizers and reviewers,

We thank you for your time. We have tried our best to address all the comments in our rebuttal. However, we withdraw our paper since some of the comments are not technically engaged with the contributions of our work. Some may require more work than what can be done in the rebuttal format. 

Thank you.

content.title: Response to reviewer 3hwY
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and questions. We address the comments below. 

> 1. “The intuition behind FUN is unclear. There is no sufficient explanations of why it works.”

We provide the intuition for FUN in the introduction on page 2, 1st paragraph. A network trained by a defender on FUN dataset is encouraged to learn the relation between class-wise filters and labels rather than useful features for classifying the clean data. While the existing unlearnability works use additive noises, FUN enjoys the advantage of introducing multiplicative noises in the Fourier domain. This lets FUN add higher amounts of noise in the image space, specifically along the edges of images, and makes it resilient to adversarial training with small additive noise budgets. 

> 2. “The variation of convolution filters is computed in an expected manner. Why can you do that?”

FUN uses convolutional filters to perturb clean images. The blur parameter controls the perturbation. Higher the blur parameter, the higher the blurring effect is. This attack is novel and different from the existing “epsilon perturbation ball” based methods that use Lp norm constraints for perturbations. Hence, a perturbation radius in terms of Lp norm is not applicable for FUN. The noises generated by the baseline unlearnability techniques require extensive training. Also, a larger perturbation budget, say in terms of $L_{\infty}$, can destroy the semantics of clean images. However, we show that the perturbations made by FUN do not break the semantics of the images.

content.title: Response to reviewer DLgf
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and questions. We address the comments below. 

> 1. “Section 3.3 presents FUN without any strong motivation.” and “why it works is not clear.”

We provide the motivation for FUN in the introduction on page 2, 1st paragraph. A network trained by a defender on FUN dataset is encouraged to learn the relation between class-wise filters and labels rather than useful features for classifying the clean data. While the existing unlearnability works use additive noises, FUN enjoys the advantage of introducing multiplicative noises in the Fourier domain. This lets FUN add higher amounts of noise in the image space, specifically along the edges of images, and makes it resilient to adversarial training with small additive noise budgets. 

> 2. “The noises of FUN are in the Fourier domain, which probably needs further explanation in the main body of the paper.”

By the convolution theorem, the convolution of two signals in the signal domain is the same as their point-wise product in the Fourier domain. We add noise by convolution in the image domain. This is equivalent to adding multiplicative noise in the Fourier domain. In Section 3.3, we discuss how FUN images are generated.

> 3. “Why FAT fails to break FUN is not explained in experiments.”

FAT fails to break FUN since the effect of FUN can be reversed only if we know the private key used to generate the random filters or have access to clean images corresponding to the FUN images. Transpose convolutions can not be used to learn such randomly generated filters without having access to clean images. We assume that the defenders do not have access to this private key and clean images.

content.title: Response to reviewer QUk3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and questions. We address the comments below. 

> 1. “The full dataset must be poisoned for the effect to be considerable.”

The full dataset need not be poisoned to obtain unlearnability with FUN. As shown in the last row of Table 5, FUN can be useful with varying data protection percentages such as 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% when trained using ERM. This experiment shows that adding a fraction of FUN images to a fraction clean dataset does not help a model learn more informative features for classification. However, we show that with adversarial training, all the unlearnability techniques (FUN and baselines) are ineffective when the full dataset is not corrupted. This shows the importance of using adversarial training in such scenarios.

> 2. “The images are visually quite different after being manipulated with FUN…”

The blurring parameter of FUN can be controlled to reduce the blurring effect. As shown in Figure 8, FUN with very low blurring (less perceptible modifications) is effective with ERM training. See Figure 6a for less perturbed FUN images. Figure 7 shows FUN images with more significant perturbations. 

> 3. “It is not obvious how this might work on non-image datasets…”

As discussed in limitations (page 9), extending FUN to other domains, such as tabular and text data, is an interesting future direction. One could generalize our framework by applying class-wise functions $g_i(x)$ to preprocess data point $x$ belonging to class $i$ such that $g_i$ is close to the identity function. Such $g_i$’s could be designed depending on the application domain. A neural network model might then learn the relationship between $g_i$ and its label $i$, instead of learning the relation between $x$ and its label. Our framework encourages models to learn the correspondence between these functions $g_i$ and labels, in contrast to prior works that add additive noises.

content.title: Response to reviewer ptSa
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and questions. We address the comments below. 

> 1. “Only ResNet18: The major weakness of the paper is mostly the experiments are performed on ResNet-18…” 

Similar to the baseline method REM, we show the transferability of FUN across various models, such as VGG-16, ResNet-18, Wide ResNet-34-10, and DenseNet-121 in Table 3. While REM noise does not transfer to all the architectures, we show that our method is successful in all the architectures we experiment with.

> 2. “The noise and perturbation budgets are not properly shown in the experiment section.”

We mention the perturbation budgets for our FUN technique and baselines in the experimental setup (Section 5.1).

> 3. “...the normalized perturbation difference images are not shown…”

We have provided the normalized perturbation difference images in Figures 6 and 7 in the Appendix.

> 4. “ This is a huge assumption as the attacker could still get a large number of clean images.”

We discuss this assumption in our limitations on page 9. A data publisher can defend this assumption by simply deleting the clean images after perturbing them.

> 5. “Fig 2, REM vs FUN, scales are not same…”

As mentioned in Appendix A.8, we use the public codebase of REM to replicate their experiments. We did not modify their hyperparameters. 

FUN does not need any training to generate the noises, as mentioned in our paper. However, REM requires solving a tri-level min-min-max optimization problem to generate unlearnable noises. Hence, noise “training time” plots for FUN are not applicable. 

The test accuracy reported for clean + ERM is the final accuracy at epoch 100. Hence it’s plotted as a dashed straight line.

> 6. “The author mentioned that "We perform experiments on REM not present in their work", ”

We mean that we performed experiments on REM with their publicly available codes to demonstrate that they can be successfully attacked with simple methods (see Section 3.2). 

> 7. Questions regarding Lemma 1

We have mentioned our theoretical setup and assumptions in Section 4. As mentioned in our future directions (page 9), it would also be interesting to see theoretical analysis of FUN considering more complex setups.

> 8. “Fourier Domain or Image Domain?, could the paper clarify whether the noise is added to the Fourier domain or actual image domain…” 

By the convolution theorem, the convolution of two signals in the signal domain is the same as their point-wise product in the Fourier domain. We add noise by convolution in the image domain. This is equivalent to adding multiplicative noise in the Fourier domain. In Section 3.3, we discuss how FUN images are generated.

> 9. “In the main paper the matrix is T(d; a, 1, a) but in the proof…”

As mentioned in the main paper and Appendix A.3, $T(d; a_y, 1, a_y) = A_y$ is the convolution matrix for class y where y is -1 or 1.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The major question that the paper tried to ponder is how to develop methods that could do some transformation on datapoints to make them unlearnable for unauthorized accesses. The method, that they called Filter-based UNlearnable (FUN) dataset generation technique, performs controlled class-wise convolutions using filters that are randomly generated and encourages the network to learn the relation between filters and labels rather than informative features for classifying the clean data. 

Contributions:
1) A fast learning approach
2) Show good results on cifar 10 and ResNet 18
3) Provided a theoretical evidence
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength
***
The paper attempted to answer the broad question of learnability of a dataset. The method tried to provide a methodology that could do the purpose with a lesser amount of time. The method shows its efficacy mostly on cifar10 and ResNet-18. 

## Weakness
***
1) __Only ResNet18__: The major weakness of the paper is mostly the experiments are performed on ResNet-18, except only one result in Table 3. While, the baseline method REM was shown on multiple models such as VGG, ResNet, WideResNet, DN-121. That majorly limits the justification of the whole work.
2) __The Perturbation__:  The noise and perturbation budgets are not properly shown in the experiment section.
3) __Writing__: The writing is very confusing. The comparison with baselines are sometime very apt, the theorem assumptions are not generalizable ( the A matrix is different in main paper and proof in the suppl. mat, the class is not binary), the normalized perturbation difference images are not shown properly and the comparison with SOTAs are missing.
4) __Assumptions__: All the images can not undergo with the same transformation or else the reverse mapping is easy. This is a huge assumption as the attacker could still get a large number of clean images. 

## Questions
***
The authors are requested to clarify the following doubts the reviewer got while reviewing the paper. The reviewer humbly request pardon if the authors find some question tone rude or harsh. 
- __Fig 2__, REM vs FUN, scales are not same for both the methods and hence the reviewer is not sure what should be observed. The REM shows all results in terms of iterations, see REM Fig 2 vs FUN Fig 2, there is no clear indication whether the authors took the exact same iterations of REM or not. Without that piece information Fig 2 of FUN is not valid. In addition to that, the REM showed training time vs FUN at testing time. The authors might verify why the test accuracy for clean is a straight line!
- __Baselines__, The author mentioned that "We perform experiments on REM not present in their work", the question is why not when the code is publicly available!
- __Lemma 1__, what would be the additional assumptions if the class is not binary but multiclass. Since all the experimental setups are multiclass wouldn't the proof be multiclass too. The [1] setup is different and hence the proof.
- __Lemma 1__, the reviewer is not sure why the 1d conv filter is set to [a,1,a] as the "1" could come to any random position, ref *A random parameter, out of the $k^2$ parameters, in each of the filters is set to have a value of 1*". Am I missing something.
- __Normalized Perturbation__, may the authors provide figures comparing normalized perturbations among SOTA methods.
- __Fourier Domain or Image Domain?__, could the paper clarify whether the noise is added to the Fourier domain or actual image domain, ref. a line in the introduction *While the existing un-learnability works use additive noises, FUN enjoys the advantage of introducing multiplicative noises in the Fourier domain*, if the noise is added to the Fourier domain then the authors are requested to show at least one figure with k-spaces. 
- __ Toeplitz Matrix__: In the main paper the matrix is T(d; a, 1, a) but in the proof in the the Suppl mat, the matrix is something different. The authors are requested to clarify it.



### Ref:
***
[1] Min et al, The curious case of adversarially robust models: More data can help, double descend, or hurt generalization. In Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, pp. 129–139. PMLR, 2021. 
[2]
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity:
*** 
1) The method is operating on image domain or Fourier is not clear. (see the line: *While the existing unlearnability works use additive noises, FUN enjoys the advantage of introducing multiplicative noises in the Fourier domain.*)
2) Why the theorem proved with binary setting when the method is for multiclass?
3) Why only ResNet 18 results are mostly shown? 
4) The comparison with REM vs FUN is not fair. The REM is not considered with its original setting despite the setup is publicly available in github

## Novelty:
*** 
I like the idea that is asking whether there could be a time efficient and reliable solution for the problem is interesting

## Reproducibility
***
I checked the code and the paper seems mostly reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposed a transformation function that could make a dataset unlearnable and prevent any kind of unauthorized accesses. The proposed method provided a comparison with the SOTA previous work REM. However, the comparisons are sometimes limited only to cifar 10 and ResNet18. The paper considers some assumption, i.e. the transformations couldn't be performed on all the datapoints, the filters are always private, etc. might not possible in real world.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the problem of creating noise for image datasets such that models learned on those datasets will perform poorly on clean testing data (indiscriminate poisoning).  Attacks that perform this task will often be ineffective on models trained on that data with adversarial training.  To perform indiscriminate poisoning that is not vulnerable to adversarial training, the paper introduces FUN, Filter-Based Unlearnable Datasets.  In this approach, each class of images is blurred with a separate, random convolutional filter.  Models trained on the resulting images display considerably worse performance on clean data, even when trained with adversarial training, or with defenses specifically designed to counteract FUN.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

- Indiscriminate data poisoning is important, and this works well empirically.
- There is theory attesting to the fact the poisoning will be effective.
- The approach is clear and easily understood.
- The approach is computationally easy to implement.

**Weaknesses**

- The images are visually quite different after being manipulated with FUN (Figures 6 and 7 from the appendix). It is not a subtle or unnoticeable approach.  The authors state that images can be blurry for many reasons, making it not detectable, but it is certainly detectable for an entire dataset to be blurry. It is also true the images are not as desirable for their original purpose when blurry.
- The full dataset must be poisoned for the effect to be considerable.
- It is not obvious how this might work on non-image datasets - perhaps the authors could speculate in rebuttal.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and easily understood.  With the details in the appendices, it seems easily reproducable.

I am not convinced the impact of this will be large.  The images are too heavily altered, the full dataset must be manipulated, and it's not clear how the approach would work on datasets that are not images.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The approach is clear, easily understood, and admirably simple.  It also works.

However, for indiscriminate poisoning to be realistic, the dataset must still be useful for its original purpose.  In this case, the blurring is too substantial for that to likely be the case.  I don't believe the theory is helpful in understanding the problem or any other poisoning results.  Therefore, the paper presents an unlikely-to-be-adopted approach, without providing further insight into any areas of research.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to construct unlearnable datasets by using class-wise filters which are expected to have a few valuable properties: 1) more robust to various data augmentations, 2) mode-free, and 3) lower computation cost.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The proposed method is simple and effective. I can easily confirm that it has properties 2&3.
2. Numerous defenses are used to verify the robustness of FUN.

Weakness:
1. Section 3.3 presents FUN without any strong motivation. Some inspiration is needed for convincement.
2. The noises of FUN are in the Fourier domain, which probably needs further explanation in the main body of the paper. I cannot sense it from the tailored class-wise filters.
3. Why FAT fails to break FUN is not explained in experiments.
4. From my understanding, FUN tries to give a universal perturbation to protect data by convolutional filters because it is model free. In other words, it is constructing transferable unlearnable examples. However, why it works is not clear.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is clearly organized, but the technique is not well-motivated. The experimental results are impressive but I did not check if that is fair for baselines.
content.summary_of_the_review: The motivation of this paper is appealing and the overall quality is good. However, I think the major contribution is not properly emphasized and supported. Empirically, the valuable properties are usually not free, but they are simply obtained by FUN, while the cost is not carefully discussed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a very lightweight "learnability attack" based on convolutional filtering against adversarial training. The proposed method does not require training. And the experimental results show that this method can successfully degrade the accuracy of the optimal Bayes classifier by poisoning Gaussian mixture data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S1: The proposed method, FUN, is very lightweight and easy to implement. 
S2: Partially proofs of the effectiveness of FUN under some limited situations (although not very practical).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
W1: The intuition behind FUN is unclear. There is no sufficient explanations of why it works.
W2: The source of the effectiveness of FUN may come from the inconsistency of the radius calculation of the epsilon perturbation ball.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The simplicity of FUN is very surprising to me. I don't understand how it works, and yet the paper did not give an in-depth explanation either. 

It seems that your "effectiveness" may come from the inconsistency of the radius calculation of the epsilon perturbation ball. In FUN, the radius of the attack epsilon ball is controlled by the magnitude of variation of convolution filters, which is very different from that calculated in existing works. The variation of convolution filters is computed in an expected manner. Why can you do that?  Will this underestimate the radius? The particularty of of the variations of different convolution filters may make the actual radius much larger than you claimed. Why don't you consider the maximum variation under a confidence interval or more directly the total pixel modification? The experiment Tables 2 & 3 should be justified to be fair in this matter.


The attack model considered in this paper is limited. For example, the NTGA can generate attack given an attack model that allows largely perturbed pixels in only a small area of an image (just like making a trigger in backdoor attack). Different attack models should be considered as baselines. And the author should discuss different existing attack models in their Related Work section. Furthermore, there should be some experiments that include other adversarial attacks and test different sizes of attack epsilon balls and norms.

Overall, this paper gives some surprising results, but they are far from convincing with the current form of presentation.

content.title: FUN: Filter-based Unlearnable Datasets
content.TL;DR: We propose a novel, model-free convolutional filter-based unlearnable dataset (FUN) generation technique that protects data from empirical risk minimization and adversarial training with various budgets.
content.abstract: Large-scale training of modern deep learning models heavily relies on publicly available data on the web. This potentially unauthorized usage of online data leads to concerns regarding data privacy. Recent works aim to make unlearnable data for deep learning models by adding small, specially designed noises to tackle this issue. However, these methods are vulnerable to adversarial training (AT) and/or are computationally heavy. In this work, we propose a novel, model-free convolutional Filter-based UNlearnable (FUN) dataset generation technique. FUN performs controlled class-wise convolutions using filters that are randomly generated via a private key. FUN encourages the network to learn the relation between filters and labels rather than informative features for classifying the clean data. We develop some theoretical analysis demonstrating that FUN can successfully poison Gaussian mixture data by reducing the clean data performance of the optimal Bayes classifier. We also empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of FUN with various datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100), and architectures (ResNet-18, VGG-16, Wide ResNet-34-10, and DenseNet-121). Our experiments show that FUN is robust to various data augmentations and training approaches such as smoothing, AT with different budgets, transfer learning, and fine-tuning. For instance, training a ResNet-18 on FUN ImageNet-100 data achieves only 8.96$\%$, 40.08$\%$, and 20.58$\%$ clean test accuracies with empirical risk minimization (ERM), $L_{\infty}$ AT, and $L_{2}$ AT, respectively. Here, ERM on the clean training data achieves a clean test accuracy of 80.66$\%$. Furthermore, we also show that FUN is robust to adaptive defenses designed specifically to break it.
